problems.description: Measured convention score is 0.73 with 12 violations, but all 8 shown violations are in files NOT touched by this commit (app.py, base_repository.py, celery_config.py, notifications.py, task_repository.py). The commit's own files (tasks_api.py, test_tasks_api.py) are PEP8-clean: snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE module constant (DEFAULT_DB_PATH), no classes. The low measured score reflects worktree context, not this diff.

test_list_tasks_ordered_desc relies on time.sleep(0.01) between creates to distinguish created_at ordering — timing-dependent and prone to flakiness; better to inject created_at explicitly or assert ordering by id DESC instead.

SonarQube cognitive complexity +30 for a greenfield CRUD module is moderately high; the single file mixes schema init, id management, and all HTTP handlers. Acceptable for Session 1 greenfield but should be decomposed as the story grows.

Manual ID counter with BEGIN IMMEDIATE adds transactional complexity versus SQLite AUTOINCREMENT; it is documented (id-reuse after deletes) and covered by test_ids_increment_manually, so it is defensible, but worth monitoring for contention in multi-connection deployments.

strengths: App-factory pattern with injectable db_path enables clean, isolated test clients against tmp_path DBs.
Manual ID counter design decision is explicitly documented in the module docstring and verified by test_ids_increment_manually.
Solid input validation on both POST and PUT (type checks plus blank/whitespace rejection) with consistent JSON error shapes.
Global JSON error handlers for 404 and 405 keep API responses uniform.
Comprehensive test coverage: create/list/get/update, validation failures, empty list, and not-found paths.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested greenfield Session 1 commit whose measured convention score of 0.73 is misleading because every listed violation lives in files outside this diff, while the commit's own code is idiomatic PEP8 Flask; architecture is sound with only minor, defensible complexities (manual ID counter, sleep-based ordering test).

problems.description: Legacy rows with owner_id=NULL are unreachable by any user — the migration comment acknowledges they become invisible 'until reassigned,' but no reassignment path exists, so pre-existing tasks are effectively orphaned (data accessibility regression).
Cognitive complexity +27 (measured) from nested auth/validation branches in require_auth, register, and login; decorator and handlers could be split into focused helpers.
SECRET_KEY falls back to a per-process secrets.token_hex(32), so JWTs invalidate on restart and break multi-worker deployments; production should require an explicitly configured secret.
AST diff shows +0 test files — the new register/login/require_auth and owner-scoped query paths have no added test coverage.

Measured convention score 0.73 with 12 violations is driven by files untouched by this commit (app.py, base_repository.py, celery_config.py, notifications.py, task_repository.py); the commit's own code is convention-clean — discrepancy between measurement and the actual diff.

strengths: Per-user task scoping applied consistently across create/list/get/update via WHERE owner_id, matching the existing query-helper pattern
Proper security hygiene: werkzeug generate_password_hash, JWT with exp/iat, no credentials in code
In-place schema migration via PRAGMA table_info that preserves pre-existing rows
Idiomatic Flask require_auth decorator that reuses get_db and extends the existing _task_to_dict pattern
Measured 0 new bugs, -1 smell, 0 duplications
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped, convention-clean auth+ownership addition that faithfully extends the app-factory/helper patterns, with minor caveats around orphaned legacy rows, a per-process fallback secret, and missing test coverage.

problems.description: Registration silently fabricates a default email ({username}@example.com) for users who supply none, and email is validated only as a non-blank string — notifications can be 'sent' to unverifiable addresses with no format/ownership check.

The completion-notification trigger (previous_status != 'completed' -> 'completed' plus enqueue) is embedded inline in the PUT /tasks/<id> handler rather than a small service/domain layer; acceptable at this size but couples the HTTP handler to notification behavior as more trigger types arrive.

The 0.73 convention score flags lowercase module-level names in celery_config.py and notifications.py, but Celery config_from_object mandates lowercase attributes (broker_url, result_backend) and logger is a standard lowercase module var — mostly checker false-positives; several flagged files (app.py, base_repository.py, task_repository.py) are also outside this diff.

Introduces a hard runtime dependency on a Redis broker (default redis://localhost:6379) for the task API; env-overridable but the app now fails to enqueue without a broker, with only a swallowed except+log in the handler.

strengths: Clean Celery layering: config (celery_config.py), app+tasks (notifications.py), Flask only imports the task signature to enqueue — a standard, idiomatic split.
DB migration for the email column mirrors the existing owner_id ALTER TABLE pattern, keeping legacy rows NULL-safe.
Trigger logic is correct: fires only on a genuine status transition to completed and uses the refetched row so a concurrent title change is reflected.
Well-tested: mocks tasks_api.send_notification_email.delay (right namespace for the imported symbol) and covers default/custom/blank email plus the completion trigger.
Failure handling around .delay() with exception logging keeps enqueue errors from failing the API request.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-architected, well-tested Celery notification feature that follows the app's existing migration and test patterns, though the 0.73 convention score partly reflects Celery-mandated lowercase config names and pre-existing files outside this diff, and the fabricated default email plus inline trigger logic are minor maintainability nits.

problems.description: BaseRepository methods (create/update/delete) call db.commit() eagerly, which contradicts the module docstring's claim that repositories 'participate in the same transaction as the rest of the request' — a route cannot roll back a failed multi-step operation if an earlier repo call already committed.

list_all() interpolates caller-supplied where/order_by strings directly into SQL with no validation; safe today only because callers pass constants, but it is a newly introduced footgun that becomes an injection vector the moment request data is passed through.

TaskRepository.update() executes an owner-scoped UPDATE but then reads the row back via get_by_id(task_id) without the owner filter; a mismatched owner_id silently returns the pre-update row as if the write succeeded, so the ownership constraint is not enforced on the read-back path.

Refactor introduces three new classes (incl. id-allocation and ownership-scoping logic) with zero new tests; behavior-preserving refactors should be covered, especially the BEGIN IMMEDIATE counter path which was moved verbatim from the route layer.

Discrepancy with measurement: the measured convention score (0.73, 12 violations) is dominated by pre-existing violations in files this commit did not touch (app.py, celery_config.py, notifications.py). Only 2 of the listed flags are in newly added files (base_repository.py, task_repository.py), and both are 'module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' — false-positive-style lints on the class attribute table_name, not genuine violations.

strengths: Centralizes ~53 lines of duplicated inline SQL from route handlers into a clean repository layer (get_by_id, list_by_owner, owner-scoped update/delete).
Preserves the existing architectural seams — raw sqlite3, shared per-request connection via Flask g, no ORM or new dependency — so the refactor stays within the codebase's established pattern.
Ownership scoping is enforced in the query layer (get_by_id_and_owner, list_by_owner), moving a security-relevant invariant into a single place.
Id allocation was moved to the owner of task creation, keeping the atomic BEGIN IMMEDIATE counter scheme intact rather than rewriting working logic.
Zero new SonarQube bugs/smells, duplications flat at 0.0%, and only +2 cognitive complexity for a 3-class abstraction — mechanically clean.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, low-risk repository-layer refactor that removes real SQL duplication and preserves the existing connection model, held back slightly by a generic SQL-interpolating helper, eager commits that contradict its own transaction docstring, and the absence of tests.

problems.description: Rate limiting adds a hardcoded runtime dependency on Redis (DEFAULT_RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI = redis://localhost:6379/2) with no requirements/storage wiring shown in the diff; flask-limiter raises on storage errors by default, so an absent or down Redis breaks every request rather than degrading gracefully.

GET /tasks response contract changes from a bare array to {data, next_cursor, total} — a breaking change for any existing consumers, with no versioning or deprecation path; existing tests had to be rewritten to match.
Cognitive complexity +32 (SonarQube smell): the cursor and limit parsing/validation blocks in list_tasks are near-duplicates; a shared _parse_pagination(request) helper would keep the handler flat.
count_by_owner runs a full COUNT(*) scan on every page request in addition to the page query; total is only UI metadata and could be dropped or made optional.

The 0.73 convention score is largely inherited: every listed violation lives in files this diff does not touch (app.py, base_repository.py, celery_config.py, notifications.py), and the sole touched file (task_repository.py) has a pre-existing constant-case violation — the commit itself introduces no new violations.

strengths: Cursor-based (keyset) pagination is correctly implemented and scoped to the repository layer, with a sound documented justification for id-DESC ordering (monotonic ids) and a correct limit+1/has_more next_cursor pattern.
Rate limiting is keyed by authenticated user id with a well-reasoned, commented fallback to IP for unauthenticated routes (e.g. /auth/login), plus a proper JSON 429 error handler.
Tests are kept isolated (memory:// storage in the fixture, fakeredis exercising the Redis backend separately) so no live Redis is needed for the suite.

New code itself is convention-clean — UPPER_CASE constants, snake_case functions, explanatory docstrings — and reuses the existing repository/factory/error-handler patterns, with the old list_by_owner cleanly renamed rather than left as dead code.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, well-tested cross-cutting commit (rate limiting + cursor pagination) that respects existing repository and factory patterns and adds no new convention violations — the 0.73 convention score is inherited from untouched files — but the hardcoded Redis rate-limit dependency and the breaking /tasks response shape are the main debts to address.

compounding_issues: Session 2 made owner_id nullable via in-place ALTER TABLE, orphaning pre-existing tasks (owner_id=NULL) with no reassignment path; the orphan problem was acknowledged in comments but never resolved in later sessions

Session 3 fabricated a default email ({username}@example.com) for registrations without email; Session 5's completion-notification trigger then 'sends' to these unverifiable addresses, compounding a data-quality decision

External dependencies accumulated silently: Session 3 hardcoded Redis as Celery broker/backend (db 0/1), Session 5 hardcoded Redis again for flask-limiter storage (db 2) — no config/requirements wiring, and flask-limiter raises on storage failure so a down Redis breaks every request (major dependency risk)

Session 1 abandoned the seed's modular Blueprint structure and left the 250-line seed app.py in the repo as permanently unimported dead code; it was never integrated or removed, lingering as an unused artifact that the convention scorer counts against every later commit
key_decisions: App-factory pattern (create_app) with injectable DB_PATH/secret_key/storage_uri/rate_limit, enabling per-test SQLite fixtures and later feature seams

Manual persisted-counter task ID allocation (BEGIN IMMEDIATE on a counters table) instead of relying on SQLite INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, which also became the foundation for cursor-based pagination via id DESC cursors
In-place ALTER TABLE migrations for each schema evolution (owner_id, users.email) rather than a migration framework, preserving legacy data through auth and notification features
Per-user task scoping via Task.owner_id keyed off the JWT subject, baking authorization into the data model from Session 2 onward

Session 4's Repository pattern (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository) as the durable data-access seam — Session 5's pagination/count logic was cleanly added to TaskRepository, keeping all SQL out of routes
Celery notification decoupled by importing only the task signature into the Flask app while the worker imports notifications.py directly, keeping the web layer async-safe
Rate limiting via flask-limiter with application_limits (shared per-user counter) and a rate_limit_key that decodes JWT independently of require_auth
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and remained high throughout. Session 1 produced a clean, idiomatic greenfield module (16 tests) that ignored the seed's Blueprint scaffolding in favor of a testable app-factory style; Session 2 layered JWT auth and per-user ownership with a forward-compatible migration, growing tests toward 62 green tests; Session 3 integrated Celery/Redis async notifications without breaking auth; Session 4 was a genuinely behavior-preserving repository refactor that moved all SQL out of routes while keeping the test suite untouched and passing; Session 5 added rate limiting and cursor pagination cleanly through the repository layer. Every session left tests green, docstrings and validation were consistently disciplined, and reviewer verdicts ran neutral-to-better. The main drag was slow accumulation of minor tech debt — orphaned legacy rows, eager commits contradicting the transaction docstring, fabricated default emails, and a growing hardcoded Redis dependency — rather than any degradation in engineering quality.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, well-disciplined 5-session arc in which each feature layered onto deliberate architectural seams (app factory, persisted-id counters, repositories) with tests green throughout, held back only by minor compounding debt around migrations, emails, and a hardcoded Redis dependency.
